newsitem.title: USA: Cyberian Outpost shuts real doors as online sales soar.
newsitem.headline: Cyberian Outpost shuts real doors as online sales soar.

text.p: - It's not often that a company shuts its doors because it's too successful, but that's what happened at Cyberian Outpost.
The Internet computer store grew so fast in the past year, the Kent, Conn., company closed a real-world retail outlet just six months after opening it.

With the online store selling $50,000 a day in computers, software and accessories, it was ludicrous to maintain a physical location that sold only $400 or $500, said Darryl Peck, the company's founder and president.

Cyberian Outpost (http://www.cybout.com) is among a pioneering group of retailers running virtual computer stores that has grown from a handful to several thousand in the past two years, according to industry estimates.
In addition to Cyberian Outpost, top contenders include Internet Shopping Network (http://www.internet.net), NECX Direct (http://necxdirect.necx.com), and Software.net (http://www.software.net/).

If the number of Internet computer vendors is starting to add up, so are online sales of computer goods. Industry analysts estimate equipment and software worth $140 million will be sold this year, climbing to $2.1 billion by 2000.

"These stores have low incremental costs and infinite shelf space. They have the potential of doing sales of $2 million per employee a year," said Jay "Marty" Tenenbaum, chairman of CommerceNet, the electronic commerce consortium. "A retail store is doing very nicely at $200,000 per employee."

Internet computer stores keep costs down by keeping warehouses empty and relying on distributors to fulfil orders for them. To compete with real-world merchants, online storefronts offer competitive prices, searchable databases, electronic shopping carts, online ordering and other interactive amenities.

Cyberian Outpost sells 9,000 items, including PCs, Macintosh computers, printers, scanners, computer memory, software, video games, computer books and related items. Sales for fiscal 1997, which ends in February, should reach $20 million, Peck said.
"It's gone way beyond our wildest dreams," he said.

After selling his software publishing company in 1994, Peck was casting around for a business to start on the World Wide Web. Software was a no-brainer. Internet users own computers or have access to them, and "the thing they'd be most inclined to buy was something for their computer," Peck said.

Peck, 37, and a crew of programmer friends built a Web store with funky, colour-splashed graphics, lots of discounts, separate "shops" for kids and videogame players, and instructions in 10 languages. Lengthy product descriptions are accompanied by pictures of software packaging, and in some cases, links to reviews.
In the early days, the company sold a lot of inexpensive game software.
"People would try us out and buy a $30 game before they'd buy a whole bunch more," Peck said.

Today, business titles sell as well as games. The company specialises in software such as Bare Bones Software's BBEdit, a hypertext markup language (HTML) editor for creating Web pages, that can't be found in the large retail chains.
"We try to pick good titles from publishers that can't afford retail channels," Peck said.

Like other online software resellers, Cyberian Outpost is experimenting with electronic delivery, allowing customers to download a programme directly from the store's Web site once they've paid for it.

Software programmes arrive encrypted, to be "opened" with a special software key once the customer's credit card has cleared. Cyberian Outpost plans to begin offering electronic delivery, using software licensed from Software.net parent Cybersource next month.
Even so, Peck isn't convinced consumers want software without a box and printed manual.

In the company's surveys, "Eight-five percent of the people said they kept the box. We were stunned by that," Peck said. "It became hugely apparent that if people want to use software they'll pirate it, but if they want to own it, they'll buy it. The problem with electronic distribution is you don't feel like you own it."
Peck is getting ready to try a few more new things. An acquisition -- Peck won't comment on the details -- is in the works and should be announced in November or December.
Peck is also getting ready to market Cyberian Outpost's underlining online store technology, although again, he won't disclose details.
"People had been asking us by the boatloads if they could buy our technology to sell their goods," he said. "After getting 50 calls a day in the spring, we said, 'There's something happening.'"
Peck said most technology available for online stores doesn't cover all the bases, a deficit that must be corrected to attract more retailers to Internet commerce.

"Running an (Internet) order business isn't trivial," he said. "We're processing hundreds of orders a day, selling 9,000 products. We're managing a lot of information. We've looked at every solution and not one could do what we needed to do."
(Michelle V. Rafter writes about cyberspace and technology from Los Angeles. Reach her at mvrafter(at)deltanet.com. Opinions expressed in this column are her own.)
